method: behavioural: four-choice olfactometer bioassay with seed odours of three weed species and a blank, choice by longest residence time; chi-square
conditions: Wild adult beetles collected with dry pitfall traps in weedy patches and canola field margins at Edmonton-area research stations (summers 2012 and 2013 per tool summary), starved 48 h, held at 21 C; four-chamber olfactometer offering 20 mg seeds of Brassica napus, Sinapis arvensis or Thlaspi arvense, or a blank control; 20 min, choice = longest residence time; absence of specific orientation or apparently random walking was scored as lack of choice; treatments were assigned randomly to the odour chambers and chamber positions were changed every five runs. Methods: 'All trials were replicated 40 times, using either imbibed or unimbibed seeds of all three weed species, each time with naive beetles' (per-species n not stated; some beetles apparently excluded from residence-time analysis). This record is the UNIMBIBED-seed four-choice test; with imbibed seeds, more P. melanarius (chi2 = 15.6, P < 0.001) and H. affinis (chi2 = 17.1, P < 0.001) responded to B. napus than to S. arvensis and T. arvense, while A. littoralis did not differ among weed species (chi2 = 2.1, P = 0.34) though its responses to all weed species differed from the blank; in two-choice tests of imbibed against unimbibed B. napus seeds all three species responded more strongly to imbibed seeds (P. melanarius chi2 = 8.10, P < 0.01; H. affinis chi2 = 6.40, P = 0.01). With unimbibed seeds more adults of all three species responded numerically to B. napus than to the other seeds, significantly only for A. littoralis (chi2 = 45, P < 0.0001). No count of non-choosing beetles is printed.

source.authors: Dylan G.E. Gomes, Holger R. Goerlitz
source.title: Individual differences show that only some bats can cope with noise-induced masking and distraction

method: behavioural: two-alternative forced choice, flat reference disc versus rippled discs (seven ripple heights) by echolocation, tested in silence and under three band-limited noise treatments; separate GLM per bat with Bonferroni correction
conditions: Captive colony at the Max Planck Institute for Ornithology, Seewiesen (the paper does not say whether the bats were wild-caught or captive-born); nine bats trained, four (three males, one female) reached criterion and were tested (two never learned the task and three learned it only somewhat; no consistent pattern with experience or age); 30 trials per ripple height and noise combination per bat (990 trials per bat). Noise was played at 70 dB SPL RMS re 20 uPa at the bat's starting position, conditions in pseudo-random order per bat, each run to completion, with a final silence retest: smooth non-overlapping (5-35 kHz), smooth-overlapping (40-90 kHz), sparse-overlapping (40-90 kHz with random silent gaps). Per tool summary of Results (not quoted): noise did not change discrimination performance of bats A and B; performance decreased for bats C and D under smooth-overlapping noise (z = -3.2, p = 0.008; z = -3.2, p = 0.004) and, in the same sentence, under sparse-overlapping noise; bat C's performance also decreased under smooth non-overlapping noise (z = -2.5, p = 0.047), bat D's did not (z = 1.8, p = 0.24); all four bats raised call sound pressure level by about 10-13 dB in overlapping noise. Sample is four trained individuals, so no population rate is implied.
quote: Additionally, we highlight that only some individuals were able to cope with noise, while others were not.

source.authors: Samuel A. Shively-Moore, B. G. Chethana Chathuprabha, Patrick A. Guerra, Stephen F. Matter
source.title: Summer Eastern North American Monarchs Do Not Use Magnetic Field for Directionality but Extreme Heat Alters Righting Behavior

method: behavioural: righting-response orientation assay inside a Helmholtz coil system, three trials per animal (pre-treatment, treatment, post-treatment); orientation tested against the 0 degree null with V-test and Rayleigh test, plus a Bayesian circular mixed-effects model
conditions: Wild adult summer monarchs of both sexes collected on the wing, 24 June to 1 September 2025, at the University of Cincinnati Center for Field Studies, Harrison, Ohio. The coils were used to keep the field consistent with the local geomagnetic field (Methods sentence read in two pieces), so the study did not rotate or otherwise alter magnetic direction (tool summary). Groups by temperature treatment: control (28 C light, 20 C dark), long-term heat (35 C light, 20 C dark after two days of acclimation), short-term heat (heat during the trial only). Per tool summary of the Results (not quoted): completed trials per group were control 14, 13, 12; long-term 27, 5, 12; short-term 5, 2, 2 (pre, during, post), because not all animals finished every trial; mean orientation did not differ from 0 degrees in every trial cell tested (the short-term treatment and post-treatment cells, N = 2 each, had no Rayleigh or V-test, and only two individuals in each of the long-term and short-term groups completed all three trials) (control pre-treatment mu = 359, r = 0.965, Rayleigh Z = 13.043, p < 0.001); the Bayesian model found no difference among treatments or trials; long-term heat reduced righting completion (Fisher exact, pre vs post p = 0.009), short-term heat had no significant effect (p = 0.273). Monarchs were clamped head-down on a vertical mesh wall (32 x 32 cm) and released; 0 degrees is the paper's expected null, a response to gravity with no orientation to the magnetic field, and northward (poleward) orientation was the expected magnetic response; the page does not give the wall's alignment to north. Light was diffused and non-directional and contained UV; the authors did not test directional light cues. Null result of a righting assay in an unaltered field with no shifted-field control, so it does not exclude magnetoreception tested by other designs (main's Wan et al. 2021 row reports a response to reversed inclination).
quote: We found that summer monarchs would right themselves, but did not use a magnetic compass to orient northward.

source.authors: C. Elisa Schaum, Robert Batty, Kim S. Last
source.title: Smelling Danger – Alarm Cue Responses in the Polychaete Nereis (Hediste) diversicolor (Müller, 1776) to Potential Fish Predation

method: behavioural bioassay: night-time emergences from artificial burrows under infrared CCTV with motion-capture software, flounder-conditioned seawater and flounder mucous in seawater, seawater control; responses scored as number of emergences, emergence duration and distance from burrow entrance
conditions: Wild harbour ragworms collected August and September 2008 from the Loch Gilp shore, Scotland, with juvenile flounder and plaice, and held in stock tanks (Methods sentence read in two pieces); worms had two days to acclimate in the experimental tanks and each worm was used only once. Worms kept in four aquaria with eight artificial burrows each, filmed night-time by infrared CCTV and scored by motion software for number of emergences, emergence duration and distance from burrow entrance; worms in a tank pooled as non-independent. Per tool summary of the paper (not read as whole sentences): bioassay 1 used flounder-conditioned seawater from 6 down to 2 fish (n = 32 worms, 16 per treatment, seven nights) with no significant reduction at 4 fish or fewer (emergence number F6,29 = 1.1, p > 0.1) and a significant reduction at 5 or more fish; bioassay 2 used flounder mucous at eight concentrations 0.1 to 1.2 ug/ml (N = 16 per treatment, three nights) with no significant reduction compared to the seawater control when flounder mucous was 0.2 ug/ml or less (number F7,34 = 2.3, duration F7,34 = 2.8, distance F7,34 = 3.1, all p > 0.1; Results sentence read verbatim by audit 345) and a significant reduction at 0.4 ug/ml and above; plaice and herring mucous gave similar responses (F2,388 = 0.48, p > 0.5); the series sit between tested steps, so 0.4 ug/ml is the lowest concentration that reduced emergence in this series, not a measured detection threshold.
quote: Using CCTV and motion capture software, we show that H. diversicolor is able to detect chemical cues associated with the presence of juvenile flounder (Platichthys flesus).
